source.version: Version of record: Proceedings of the Design Society, Volume 5: ICED25, pp. 429-438, doi 10.1017/pds.2025.10057, published online by Cambridge University Press. All 10 PDF pages read from the PDF on file.
source.title_on_document: AI vs. human: exploring the potential of generative AI as a feedback tool to support ideation in design education

paper_design_summary: Twenty-five students from four Bavarian universities each wrote one startup idea to reduce academic stress in Round 01 (Crazy 8s, then a 15-minute refinement), before any feedback; AI use during ideation was not stated. Each idea then received two written feedback comments, one from GPT-4 and one from a human lecturer, and students read both in a randomized order (13 human first, 12 AI first). Students rated each feedback comment in surveys using both five-point Likert and three-point responses (social-emotional perception, encouragement and inspiration, coherence, structure) and were interviewed; no creative output was scored.

studies.label: Within-subjects comparison of GPT-4 versus lecturer feedback on a startup ideation task

assignment.what_was_assigned: The order in which each student read the two feedback comments on their own idea (human lecturer first or GPT-4 first). Every student received both comments. The idea was written in Round 01, before any feedback; AI use during ideation was not stated. No post-feedback revision or creativity score was reported.
assignment.quote: In Round 03, students received both AI- and human-generated feedback, with the order randomized to minimize bias—13 students received human feedback first, while 12 received AI feedback first.
assignment.locator: PDF p. 3 (printed p. 431), Section 3.1 Study design; Figure 1, annotation under 'Core experiment'

arms.name: AI feedback (GPT-4), 'Feedback comment B'
arms.description: 150-word structured critique of the student's idea generated by GPT-4 with an optimized prompt and a standardized feedback form (strengths, improvement areas, further development). Received by all 25 students; 12 read it first.

arms.name: Human lecturer feedback, 'Feedback comment A'
arms.description: 150-word structured critique of the same idea by one of six human educators (five professors and one lecturer) using the same form. Received by all 25 students; 13 read it first.

participants.exclusions: None reported for students: 25 completed surveys and 25 interviews. Section 3.4 says incomplete submissions were discarded but gives no count.
participants.who: University students from the 5th Bachelor's semester to the 3rd Master's semester in human factors engineering, architecture, computer science, HCI, design leadership, industrial design, mechanical engineering, and business administration. Feedback givers were six educators from two German universities (abstract: 'six human educators'; conclusion: 'five human professors, and one lecturer').
participants.quote: In total, 25 students from four universities in Bavaria, Germany, were recruited. ... The outcome was 25 completed surveys and 25 transcribed interview recordings for further analysis.
participants.locator: PDF p. 4 (printed p. 432), Section 3.3 Participant recruitment; PDF p. 3 (printed p. 431), Section 3.1; abstract PDF p. 1 (n=25)

ai_tool.how_used: The researchers, not the students, prompted GPT-4 to write a 150-word critique of each submitted idea using a standardized feedback form. Students only read the output; they did not interact with the AI.

task.description: Develop a practical, new, and feasible startup idea that helps students reduce their stress, using 'Crazy 8s' (eight ideas in eight minutes) and then documenting one idea in a written template.
task.duration: 8 minutes of ideation plus a 15-minute refinement phase with an optional extension

outcomes.name: Social-emotional perception of the feedback (positivity, supportiveness, fairness, competence, overall)
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Student ratings of each feedback comment. H1 specifies a 5-point Likert scale for positivity, supportiveness, fairness, and competence, but does not specify the scale for the overall item. Section 3.4 describes both 5-point Likert and 3-point responses without a complete item-to-scale mapping (PDF p. 5, Sections 3.4 and 4 H1; Figure 3, PDF p. 6). H1 tested AI ratings against a 3.0 benchmark; H5 compared AI and lecturer feedback with a Wilcoxon signed-rank test. The ideas themselves were never scored.

contrasts.reported: AI feedback: 'Positivity and supportiveness received median values 5.00 (p = 0.002, p < 0.05)' against the 3.0 benchmark. AI vs human: 'The Wilcoxon signed-rank test revealed significant differences in social-emotional perception and overall feedback ratings'; arm distributions shown only as boxplots in Figure 3.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 5 (printed p. 433), Section 4 H1; PDF p. 6 (printed p. 434), H5 and Figure 3

outcomes.name: Perceived encouragement and inspiration of the feedback (positivity, encouragement, inspiration, overall)
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Four survey questions on encouragement and inspiration (PDF p. 6, Section 4 H2). The H2 paragraph does not specify their response scales; Section 3.4 reports both 5-point Likert and 3-point responses without a complete item-to-scale mapping (PDF p. 5).

contrasts.reported: AI feedback: 'Both measures had a first quartile of 4.00 ... while median values were 4.00 and 5.00. H2 was validated as AI feedback surpassed the 3.0 threshold for all sub-aspects (p = 0.002, p < 0.05).' AI vs human: Wilcoxon signed-rank 'significant results (p < 0.05) across all sub-aspects'; boxplots in Figure 3.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 6 (printed p. 434), Section 4 H2 and Figure 3; PDF p. 7 (printed p. 435), H5

outcomes.name: Perceived coherence of the feedback (correctness, context fit, conclusiveness, order, detail, overall)
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Six survey questions on coherence (PDF p. 6, Section 4 H3). The H3 paragraph does not specify their response scales; Section 3.4 reports both 5-point Likert and 3-point responses without a complete item-to-scale mapping (PDF p. 5). Figure 3 panel titles appear swapped: the panel labelled 'Coherence perception (H3)' shows structure items and the panel labelled 'Structure and outer perception (H4)' shows coherence items.

contrasts.reported: AI feedback: 'Median ratings were high across all sub-aspects, with correctness at 5.00, context fit at 5.00, and conclusiveness at 5.00. No sub-aspects fell below 3.0 ... (p = 0.006, p < 0.05).' AI vs human: Wilcoxon signed-rank p < 0.05 across all sub-aspects; boxplots in Figure 3.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 6 (printed p. 434), Section 4 H3 and Figure 3; PDF p. 7 (printed p. 435), H5

eligibility.reason: The study analyzed 25 students, below the 50-person threshold (PDF p. 3, Section 3.1; p. 4, Section 3.3). Only the order in which students read GPT-4 and lecturer feedback was randomized, after their ideas were written in Round 01; AI use during ideation was not stated (PDF p. 3, Section 3.1 and Figure 1). No comparison of creative outputs produced under randomized AI-assistance conditions was reported. Outcomes were students' self-reported perceptions of feedback; creativity or diversity was not scored on their ideas (PDF p. 5, Section 3.4; pp. 5-7, Section 4 and Figure 3). Under codebook Section 3, this small perception study belongs only in the screening report.

one_line_finding: In a within-subjects study of 25 students, GPT-4 feedback on their startup ideas was rated higher than lecturer feedback on every perception scale (Wilcoxon signed-rank p < 0.05 across all sub-aspects, PDF p. 7; boxplots in Figure 3, PDF p. 6), but idea creativity was not measured.
